scams.name: Wyndham / Timeshare 'Free Theme Park Tickets' Presentation Trap
scams.description:
This is the most-complained-about scam on traveler reports. The thread 'What's the deal with those cheap discount theme park tickets' (o1odlx) is blunt: 'It's just Wyndham tours running a time share scam, they ask you attend a 5 hour conference in exchange for discounted theme park tickets.' traveler reports 'Timeshare - locked in for 64 years!!' (k2iw80). traveler reports 'Did I just get scammed?' (k0zlhz) has the hindsight observation: 'Our Gold coast holidays were always subsidised by timeshare... Google wyndham timeshare scam and look at the reviews.' ACCC and NSW Fair Trading have issued repeated consumer warnings about Gold Coast timeshare sales tactics.

Your fix is absolute: do not engage with anyone offering 'free' or 'discounted' theme park tickets in exchange for attending a presentation. Buy theme park tickets through the official Village Roadshow Theme Parks multi-park pass (themeparks.com.au) or direct from Dreamworld (dreamworld.com.au). Multi-park passes are genuinely discounted and include no obligation. If you've already signed a timeshare contract, use the cooling-off period (7 business days in QLD) to rescind in writing; after that, consult a consumer lawyer — vacation-club contracts are notoriously difficult to unwind.

Multi-park passes are genuinely discounted and include no obligation. Buy theme park tickets through Village Roadshow Theme Parks multi-park pass or direct from each park; Decline every 'free ticket' offer from street recruiters — the presentation itself is the product; If attending a presentation anyway, bring a phone alarm set for 90 minutes and leave when it rings; Never sign any contract on the day of a presentation — use the QLD 7-day cooling-off period; Check Consumer Affairs QLD (qld.gov.au/law/fair-trading) for current vacation-club warnings
scams.location: Surfers Paradise streets, Cavill Avenue, hotel lobbies, roadside booths near theme parks
scams.tldr: A cheerful recruiter on Cavill Avenue offers you 'discounted' two-day theme park passes to Warner Bros Movie World and Sea World — all you have to do is attend a 90-minute 'holiday club presentation' tomorrow morning. You show up; the 90-minute session stretches to 5 hours. High-pressure sales close you into a 'vacation club' contract that will cost tens of thousands over decades, supposedly 'saving' you money on future holidays.

scams.name: Gold Coast Airport (OOL) Taxi Overcharge
scams.description:
A traveler threads titled 'Was I scammed by the taxi driver?' (1jchuev);I got charged $360 to go from Gold Coast airport to 10 minutes up the road.' The traveler threads 'Airport taxi and rideshare scams you need to know about' (1h1f0ns);Taxi drivers who overcharge passengers, refuse short trips or refuse to use the pay meter are at risk of being chucked out of the industry — at least in NSW.' Queensland enforcement is weaker, and Gold Coast Airport is one of the worst hot spots in the state. traveler reports 'Taxi scam Australia' (1nmif8j) echoes: taxi drivers routinely quote flat fares of $20–60 for trips that should be $5–15 metered.

Your best defense is Uber or DiDi from the OOL rideshare bay, or pre-booked airport transfer via your hotel. Con-X-ion Gold Coast Airport Shuttle runs regular shared services to all major Gold Coast hotels for $25–35 per person — the tourist-proof option. If you must take a taxi, insist the meter is visible and running before the taxi pulls away, pay by card on the in-car terminal, and photograph your receipt. Report overcharging to Queensland Translink and the Personalised Transport Ombudsman.

scams.location: Gold Coast Airport (Coolangatta/OOL) arrivals, Tugun taxi rank
scams.tldr: You arrive at Gold Coast Airport after a short interstate flight. You grab a taxi for what should be a 15-minute drive to your Surfers Paradise hotel. The driver works an unclear route, disputes the meter, and demands $360 in cash at drop-off. The Uber estimate for the same trip is $45.

scams.name: Fake / Unauthorised Theme Park Ticket Discount Sites
scams.description: You Google 'Dreamworld cheap tickets' and a site near the top of the results offers a 3-park pass for $99 (normally $179). The design is polished. You pay by card. On the day, the QR code doesn't scan at the Dreamworld gate. Customer support is an overseas call centre that hangs up when you describe the problem.
scams.avoidance: Your safe path is to buy through the parks' official channels: themeparks.com.au (Village Roadshow for Movie World, Sea World, Wet'n'Wild, Paradise Country), dreamworld.com.au (Dreamworld, WhiteWater World, SkyPoint). A legitimate Village Roadshow multi-park 'Super Pass' with real discount is sold on their site. Avoid Thrillopilia, ticketstodo and similar aggregators you can't verify with the parks themselves. If you've already bought from a suspicious site and the QR doesn't scan, chargeback on your credit card is your primary recourse. Buy direct from themeparks.com.au (Village Roadshow) and dreamworld.com.au; Use Village Roadshow's Super Pass for genuine multi-park discounts; If using a third party, stick to Klook, Viator or GetYourGuide (vetted operators); Pay by credit card for chargeback protection; Verify QR codes on the parks' official apps before the visit day
scams.location: Google Ads targeting 'Dreamworld tickets', 'Movie World cheap tickets', 'Sea World discount'

scams.name: Cavill Avenue Nightclub Wristband & Tab Scam
scams.description:
The traveler threads 'Nightclub scammer??' (16id9zs) has the mechanism verbatim: 'A dude handing nightclub info he's offered to sell us wristbands for $60 a night that give us entry to a bunch of the clubs and one drink at each of them... It's not a scam but it's also not the most popular night clubs.' The follow-ups confirm that many of the affiliated venues are half-empty secondary bars — the real clubs (Vanity, Sin City, Bedroom, etc.) have no wristband partnership with random street promoters. The second variant is inside-club: tab inflation, 'accidental' extra drinks, or card readers that seem to tap multiple times on close-out. traveler reports 'Have you ever been scammed at a bar/club?' (1onwgr3) has the Gold Coast data point: 'That's $119 she and the bartender were scamming me of. I asked for a refund but their security kicked me out.'

Your defense is to buy club entry only at the door, pay the listed cover in cash or on a card tap, and keep your receipts. Most Surfers Paradise clubs are free to enter before midnight and charge a $20–$30 cover after — that's the total cost, not a $60 wristband-for-multiple-clubs deal. Use 'tab transparency' never hand your card to a bartender to 'start a tab' unless you can see every charge on the reader before you leave.

Use 'tab transparency' — never hand your card to a bartender to 'start a tab' unless you can see every charge on the reader before you leave. Pay cover only at the door of a specific named club — no multi-club wristband product is legitimate; Keep your card in your wallet — tap each round individually rather than opening an open tab; Scrutinise every charge on the in-club receipt before signing; If overcharged, stay calm, request the manager and photograph the bill; If refunded unfairly denied, chargeback on your credit card the next day
scams.location: Cavill Avenue, Orchid Avenue, Surfers Paradise clubbing strip
scams.tldr: A young 'promoter' on Cavill Avenue approaches your group and offers $60 wristbands — one per person — that give you entry to 'a bunch of clubs' plus one drink each. It sounds efficient. You pay cash for four wristbands. At the first club the wristband 'isn't recognized this week.' At the second the door staff say they've never had a wristband arrangement. Your $240 is gone and nobody is ever at fault.

scams.name: Fake Short-Stay Apartment Listing (Surfers / Broadbeach / Burleigh)
scams.description:
traveler reports 'Scam?' (1n6gh7l);I'm in Gold Coast and I try to see if the guy who want to rent me the flat is a scam?..' traveler reports 'There's scams on all legitimate rental sites now' (1gsdj89);He was renting out a house in Gold Coast via Gumtree, which normally...' traveler reports 'Urgent Seeking Community Advice on Suspected Rental Scam' (18ti14g) has similar Queensland patterns. The scammers target Surfers, Broadbeach and Burleigh because demand is year-round and short-stay stock is huge — a few fake listings blend in easily.

Your defense is identical to the Sydney/Melbourne rule: book only via the official Airbnb or Booking.com app, never pay outside the platform, reverse image-search listing photos, check for reviews from multiple guests in the past 12 months, and request a 60-second live video call before paying. Gold Coast-specific: verify apartment numbers against real buildings on Google Street View — scammers often cite famous buildings (Q1, Soul, Hilton Surfers) but list a unit number that isn't in the building's floor plan.

Book only through airbnb.com or booking.com via the app or a bookmarked URL; Never pay by bank transfer outside the platform; Reverse image-search photos in Google Images; Verify the building and apartment number on Google Street View; Require 3+ reviews in the past 12 months before paying
scams.location: Airbnb / Booking.com clones, Gumtree, Facebook Marketplace
scams.tldr: You find a beachfront apartment in Broadbeach on a slick-looking rental site — $170/night for a week, incredible ocean-view photos, the host explains Airbnb fees 'inflate the price' and asks for bank transfer. You send $1,190. When you arrive, the building is real, but the apartment number doesn't exist. The site is down. Emails bounce.

scams.name: Jet Ski / Scooter / Beach-Toy Damage Scam
scams.description:
The jet-ski and beach-toy phantom damage scam is well-documented globally (famously in Phuket, Bali and Mexico) and has its Australian variant on the Gold Coast. traveler reports 'Asking for advice after getting a rented jetski damaged' (1kjmer8) comment: 'This is a common scam at international tourist destinations. Are you sure you actually damaged the hull?' traveler reports 'Did we deserve to lose the $500 security deposit on an...' (o4n4lu): 'Common scam. You could try small claims court, but if...' The operator's leverage is your credit card hold; if you dispute, they keep the card charge and complicate your departure.

Your defense is full video documentation before use. Before starting the jet ski, scooter or hire-boat, video every surface, every scratch, every wear pattern. Date and timestamp in the video. At return, record again before handing back the keys and ask the operator to confirm 'no new damage' on the video. If a dispute arises, your video is evidence. Pay with a credit card (never debit) so you can chargeback; Australian chargebacks for disputed rental damage routinely succeed when there's video evidence.

Video-walk the jet ski or scooter at pickup AND return — all surfaces, timestamped; Insist on a signed no-damage receipt before walking away; Pay by credit card (not debit) for chargeback protection; Read TripAdvisor reviews specifically for damage-charge complaints before booking; Choose established operators (Gold Coast Jetski, Jet Boat Extreme) over one-booth street hirers
scams.location: Surfers Paradise foreshore, The Spit, Broadwater jet-ski hire booths
scams.tldr: You hire a jet ski at The Spit for a 30-minute session — $180 with a $500 security deposit. At return, the operator points out a new scratch on the hull you're certain wasn't your doing. He keeps the full deposit and adds a $750 'repair' charge on your card.
